chapters.title: The Impossible Observation
chapters.text:
Albert Einstein built modern physics on one unbreakable rule: nothing in the universe can travel faster than the speed of light. Not a rocket, not a radio signal, not even a single subatomic particle.

Yet right now, the James Webb Space Telescope is staring straight at a real galaxy — known as JADES-GS-z14-0 — that is racing away from Earth at more than twice the speed of light. And it isn't some rare glitch. Most of the galaxies visible in our night sky are receding faster than light right this second.

So how can entire galaxies outrun light without shattering Einstein's most famous law? And even stranger: if they are moving away faster than light, how did their light ever reach our telescopes in the first place?

The answer forces you to separate two completely different kinds of motion — and once you see the difference, you'll realize why roughly ninety-five percent of the galaxies we can see tonight are already gone from our reach forever.

chapters.title: What Einstein Actually Forbade
chapters.text:
To solve the paradox, we have to look closely at what Einstein's nineteen-oh-five theory of special relativity actually bans.

Picture a spacecraft firing its engines in empty space. As it pushes faster and faster toward three hundred thousand kilometers per second, special relativity says the energy needed to speed it up climbs toward infinity. The fabric of space itself acts like an unbreakable speed limit for anything traveling through space.

So if no engine, explosion, or force can push a galaxy past the speed of light, what on Earth is accelerating distant galaxies past it?

The surprising answer is: nothing is pushing them through space at all.

Ten years after special relativity, Einstein published general relativity — a far bigger theory where space isn't a rigid, fixed stage. Space itself can bend, curve, and stretch. And in nineteen twenty-seven, physicist Georges Lemaître realized Einstein's equations predicted an expanding universe — a prediction Edwin Hubble confirmed just two years later in nineteen twenty-nine when he measured distant galaxies drifting away from us in every direction.

Those galaxies aren't rocketing through space faster than light. Instead, the space between us and them is stretching — creating brand-new space every single second.

chapters.title: The Expanding Grid & The Rubber Band
chapters.text:
To see how stretching space breaks the light-speed barrier without breaking Einstein, imagine placing galaxies on the grid lines of a giant elastic sheet.

Pin our Milky Way to one intersection, and pin a chain of distant galaxies down the line. Notice that every galaxy stays parked right on its own grid point. Locally, none of them are racing through space at all.

Now stretch the grid uniformly. Every single square grows slightly wider at the exact same rate — roughly sixty-seven kilometers per second for every three-point-three million light-years of distance.

For a nearby galaxy just one grid square away, that stretch is tiny — nowhere near light speed. For a galaxy two squares away, two stretches add up, so it separates twice as fast. Three squares away, three times as fast. That simple pattern is Hubble's Law: the farther away a galaxy sits, the more stretching space lies between us, and the faster the gap grows.

Keep stacking enough grid squares side by side, and eventually the combined expansion adds up to more than three hundred thousand kilometers per second.

You can picture the exact same trick with an ant walking along a rubber band. Suppose the ant's absolute top speed is one centimeter per second — its own unbreakable speed limit. Now pull both ends of the rubber band apart at five centimeters per second. At every moment, the ant never cheats; its feet still crawl over the rubber right underneath it at one centimeter per second. Yet the opposite end of the rubber band is receding five times faster than the ant can walk.

Galaxies obey the exact same rule: nothing ever outruns a beam of light passing right beside it locally. General relativity simply puts no speed limit on how fast empty space itself can expand.

chapters.title: How Light Swims Upstream
chapters.text:
That cleanly saves Einstein's speed limit — but it immediately leaves us with our second, even stranger puzzle.

Draw a giant sphere around Earth at a radius of fourteen-point-four billion light-years. Astronomers call this boundary the Hubble Sphere. Right on that line, expanding space carries galaxies away from us at exactly the speed of light. Beyond fourteen-point-four billion light-years, galaxies recede faster than light.

So pause and ask a natural question: if a galaxy outside that sphere shines a beam of light toward Earth today, isn't that light automatically swept backward forever?

Remarkably, the answer is no — and this is one of the most common misconceptions in all of astronomy.

Follow a single photon emitted toward Earth from a galaxy fifteen-point-five billion light-years away. Because space there is receding faster than light, the photon loses ground at first. Even though it travels forward through local space at full light speed, the expanding fabric drags it farther away from Earth!

So how can it possibly make it home? Because the expansion rate of the universe per unit distance — the Hubble parameter — is actually decreasing over time. As it drops, you have to look farther out to find space receding at light speed. In other words, the Hubble Sphere itself is growing outward!

As the photon keeps swimming upstream at light speed, the expanding Hubble Sphere eventually overtakes it. The instant that boundary passes the photon, space around it is now receding slower than light. The photon stops drifting backward, starts closing the distance to Earth, and billions of years later hits a telescope mirror.

If watching a beam of light literally get rescued by an expanding cosmic boundary just blew your mind, take a quick second to hit that like button — it really helps visual physics explainers reach more curious viewers.

chapters.title: The Real Point of No Return
chapters.text:
Wait a second. If the Hubble Sphere keeps growing outward to rescue photons, does that mean light from any distance will eventually reach us if we just wait long enough?

No — and to see why, bring back our ant on the rubber band.

If you stretch a rubber band at a steady, constant rate, a shocking piece of math takes over: even if the far end moves away ten times faster than the ant can walk, the ant will still eventually reach the other side, because each step permanently locks in a tiny fraction of the band.

Now change just one thing: instead of stretching steadily, accelerate the stretch exponentially — so every meter of rubber doubles in size over a fixed interval of time. Suddenly, the newly created rubber ahead of the ant explodes faster than the ant can ever claim a meaningful fraction of it. Beyond a sharp cutoff distance, the ant is trapped forever.

In nineteen ninety-eight, astronomers discovered that our universe behaves like that second rubber band. Driven by dark energy, the expansion of space is accelerating.

Because of dark energy, our Hubble Sphere won't keep growing forever — it will max out around seventeen-point-five billion light-years. That locks in a true point of no return called the Cosmic Event Horizon, sitting roughly sixteen-point-five billion light-years away today.

A photon leaving a galaxy at fifteen-point-five billion light-years today will still be rescued and reach Earth. A photon leaving a galaxy at seventeen billion light-years today never will — no matter how many trillions of years it travels.

chapters.title: Why We Can Still See 46.5 Billion Light-Years
chapters.text:
Now everything clicks together into three nested shells centered on Earth.

First, at fourteen-point-four billion light-years, sits the Hubble Sphere — where recession speed crosses the speed of light today.

Just outside it, at sixteen-point-five billion light-years, sits the Cosmic Event Horizon — the absolute cutoff for any light leaving a galaxy right now.

Yet our Observable Universe reaches all the way out to forty-six-point-five billion light-years in every direction — ninety-three billion light-years across!

How can we see JADES-GS-z14-0, which sits thirty-three-point-eight billion light-years away right now — more than twice as far as our cosmic event horizon?

Because we aren't seeing light it emitted today. We are catching ancient light it emitted thirteen-point-five billion years ago, when the young universe was tiny and that galaxy sat barely two billion light-years from our neighborhood. Its photons were swept up by our expanding Hubble Sphere early in cosmic history and began making their way toward us. During the thirteen-point-five billion years those photons spent crossing space, expansion carried the galaxy itself all the way out to thirty-three-point-eight billion light-years away.

We are seeing its ancient baby photo — even though the light it is shining right now will never reach us.

chapters.title: The Lonely Cosmic Future
chapters.text:
Step back and look at the volume of those two spheres side by side.

The reachable region inside our sixteen-point-five-billion-light-year event horizon makes up only about five percent of the volume of the observable universe. That means roughly ninety-five percent of all the galaxies we can see through telescopes tonight are already permanently beyond our reach. Even if we launched a beam of light straight toward them right this second, it would never arrive.

And over the next hundreds of billions of years, dark energy will keep carrying distant galaxies across that event horizon one by one. Their light will stretch into longer, dimmer red wavelengths until they fade completely into darkness.

Trillions of years from now, only the galaxies bound together by gravity — our own Milky Way merged with Andromeda and our closest neighbors — will remain in the sky, surrounded by an empty black void.

Nothing ever broke Einstein's speed limit. Space simply grew larger than light could ever outrun.
